key_findings.claim: Sections 3–4 pp. 3–6: CNN features are projected using depth into a ground-plane map M in R^(C×Y×X), updated by sparse convolutional GRU. An LSTM instruction decoder emits successive action and observation descriptions. A differentiable histogram Bayes filter represents ghost pose (x,y,heading). The motion update convolves the previous belief with instruction/map-dependent normalized kernels (Eqs.3–4); a LingUNet observation likelihood multiplies this prior and the posterior is renormalized (Eq. 5). Six inner filter steps infer the whole instruction trajectory and are rerun whenever the real agent expands its map. A separate MLP scores observed graph nodes using belief neighborhood, distance and visited flag; selecting a visited node stops. Training minimizes KL to demonstrated instruction-trajectory beliefs plus teacher-action cross-entropy, with a 50:50 teacher/policy mixture; visual CNN is frozen. Inference repeatedly maps real views, reinfers the ghost's endpoint and chooses reachable nodes. No online model gradients or RGB synthesis.

key_findings.claim: Section 3 pp. 3–5 Eqs.2–3: first generate a future image from current image and instruction, then predict a short action chunk conditioned on that subgoal. VILA-U7B encodes 256×256 images as 16×16 positions with four residual codes each. Vision tower is frozen; language backbone, projector and depth transformer are trained. Causal visual-token CE (Eq. 4) plus full-attention action-token CE (Eq. 5) form Eq. 6. Each of seven action dimensions is discretized into 256 bins between training-data 1 st/99 th percentiles; ten-action chunks are predicted in parallel from special placeholders. Pretraining mixes selected OpenX robot data with action-free EPIC-KITCHENS and Something-SomethingV2 for visual targets; downstream task demonstrations fine-tune the same modules. Algorithm 1 generates subgoal, executes the chunk, obtains a genuine new observation and repeats. It does not observe intermediate outcomes during the whole chunk. The hybrid attention distinction affects latency and must be controlled separately from visual reasoning.

Table 1 p. 5 LIBERO average 81.13±0.6 versus OpenVLA76.5±0.6 across three seeds and 500 episodes per suite; Long 69.0 versus 53.7, Object 91.6 versus diffusion-policy 92.5. Thus not uniformly best. Bridge tasks use ten trials per task, and separate Franka models use 10–150 demonstrations per task (pp. 5–6). The abstract's relative gains should not be mistaken for percentage-point gains. No navigation experiment or independent execution. Table 3, p. 8 tests two novel tasks with five trials each: generated goal images yield 20%/0% success, while demonstration goal images yield 60%/40%. This small privileged-goal intervention supports a subgoal-quality bottleneck. Section 5 reports approximately sevenfold inference slowdown at chunk length ten due to generating 256 visual tokens, and acknowledges missing high-frequency feedback between chunk boundaries.

Subgoals can be visually plausible but unreachable, and long chunks delay correction. Extra actionless data, backbone and full attention are material confounders. A good generated picture is not a calibrated physical counterfactual. Public project was located; complete released training/evaluation implementation not yet verified.

key_findings.claim: Sections 3–5: an (m,b)-VAML objective compares model value after m imagined transitions with a b-step bootstrapped real target. For independent real/model samples, Eq. 3 decomposes sample squared error into desired squared expected-value error plus model-value variance and target variance. The model variance term changes the optimum. CVAML subtracts an estimated model-value variance, requiring multiple model samples, to recover the intended expectation objective; finite-sample normalization must match the source implementation. The value learner is separately trained with ordinary TD (m=0) because stochastic MuZero-style imagined-target regression can fail even with perfect dynamics. Eq. 7 explains why latent feature MSE targets E[φ(s')] while value matching targets E[V (φ(s'))]; they commute for all distributions only with affine V. Proposition 5 gives existence of deterministic value-equivalent models under compact connected metrizable state space, continuous kernel/value and bijective latent mapping. It neither proves learnability nor guarantees arbitrary downstream rewards or policies. Training/inference otherwise inherit MuZero-style model-based RL agents; no picture generation is required. Appendix A.3, pp. 18–20, proves existence by continuity on a compact connected latent image and a measurable selection attaining the expected value. This supplies a measurable value-equivalent mapping for one fixed value function, not a continuous neural realization or a model preserving all language-conditioned values.

Figures 2–3 pp. 6–8 evaluate 1000 randomly generated Garnet MDPs with bootstrap intervals and seven challenging DMC dog/humanoid tasks with 30 seeds. Improvements depend on setting; not a universal dominance theorem. The finite-MDP experiments test the identified bias more directly than aggregate DMC return. No R2R/RxR or physical navigation validation is provided. Figure 4, p. 9 explicitly aggregates 30 seeds per environment. Appendix Table 2, p. 21 specifies latent width 512, batch 128, discount 0.99, actor/critic/model learning rates 3e-4, encoder rate 1e-4, one-step model rollout, and one/four model samples. Appendix C.4, p. 23 shows the BYOL-style auxiliary loss is essential in its humanoid experiments: objective calibration alone is insufficient.

Correction requires extra samples and can increase estimator variance; value equivalence is policy/reward dependent, so preserving current V can discard information needed after a language-goal change. Existence conditions do not establish an implementable globally correct navigation model. Calibration here means objective correction, not action-risk reliability or conformal coverage.

key_findings.claim: INSPECTED CODE: `mad_td/training_util/model_loss_functions.py:120–171` evaluates sampled model next states using the critic, subtracts a variance correction, and minimizes squared mismatch of sample-mean values. Lines 156–158 use population sample variance (`ddof=0`) divided by N. Under the restricted assumption of independent samples and a fixed value function, an unbiased correction would use unbiased sample variance divided by N; this implementation leaves a sigma²/N² residual. Its action may depend on the first sampled next state, so the simple independent-sample derivation is not a general diagnosis of training behavior. Lines 390–425 show objective dispatch and target-critic use. `config/algo/corrected_itervaml.yaml` uses four stochastic samples and retains likelihood-related model losses. `mad_td/trainers/mad_td_model.py:40–95` initializes encoder, actor, critic and latent-model train states from replay data. `mad_td/utils/eval_utils.py:25–50` evaluates on-policy one-step tuples using saved physics state. The isolated iid fixed-value finite-sample variance correction check finds expected residual loss 0.0625 for N=4 Rademacher samples; unbiased sample variance correction is approximately zero. This is not a CVAML benchmark run.

key_findings.claim: Section 3 pp. 3–5: frozen DINOv2 encodes an image into N spatial patches of width E, z∈R^(N×E). Inference uses receding-horizon CEM: sample action sequences, roll out latent predictions, score terminal feature MSE to the goal, refit elite action distributions, execute the first action and replan using a real image. key_findings.claim: Section 3 pp. 3–5: recurrent state-space model has deterministic history and stochastic latent state; observation posterior is fit to a transition prior. World-model training uses pixel/reward likelihood and KL (Eqs.9–10), with contrastive/reward-only variants examined. From posterior states, imagination generates trajectories using the learned actor and transition model. Lambda returns (Eq. 6) combine truncated reward sequences with bootstrapped values. Actor maximizes these returns through differentiable/reparameterized dynamics (Eq. 7); critic regresses stop-gradient lambda targets (Eq. 8). Dynamics parameters are held fixed during behavior updates, while gradients propagate through their operations into actor actions. At deployment real images update the posterior and the actor selects an action; there is no online CEM tree search. Data collection, model fitting and imagined actor/critic learning alternate.

Figure 6 p. 6 reports mean score 823 after 5 M environment steps across 20 DMC tasks, compared with PlaNet 332 and D4PG786 after 100 M; five seeds. The comparison supports sample efficiency in this suite, not equal compute or language navigation performance. Representation/return-horizon ablations show contributions, but no formal off-distribution guarantee.

A policy can exploit model errors outside collected support; differentiable long rollouts can amplify model and value bias. Reward reconstruction can omit task-relevant details when future goals change. The learned policy removes online search cost but shifts cost into imagined training and an imperfect value model.

key_findings.claim: Section 3 and Algorithm 1, pp. 3–4: prompt an LLM for outlier class names that are visually related but distinct from known classes. Far, near and fine-grained settings use different prompts. Remove lexical overlap, embed known and envisioned labels with CLIP, and compare them to the normalized image embedding. Equation 3 subtracts beta times the largest envisioned-outlier softmax probability from the largest known-class probability; the softmax denominator includes both sets and beta is 0.25. Threshold the resulting scalar for ID/OOD classification. Evaluation reports false positives at a threshold chosen to retain 95% of ID examples. There is no task-specific model training, dynamics model, action policy or future rollout. CLIP pretraining and offline LLM generation remain external dependencies.

Table 1, p. 5 averages four ID datasets and four OOD datasets: FPR95 0.21/AUROC 99.92 versus MCM 2.68/99.40. CLIPN uses extra data and scores 0.67/99.80. Later results are substantially harder: the ImageNet far-OOD result on pp. 6–8 has FPR95 30.09/AUROC 92.96; near-OOD average is 9.07/98.59; the fine-grained average is 60.52/81.82 versus CLIPN 56.05/83.18. Thus near-perfect small-dataset numbers must not be generalized to all settings. These are paper experiments, not executed reproduction.

Generated negative labels cannot enumerate all unknown appearances. The ImageNet20 near-OOD setting filters semantic cosine overlap at 0.85, but this does not guarantee coverage of unseen categories or semantic disjointness elsewhere. LLM versions and prompts alter candidate lists. An unsafe or instruction-inconsistent navigation action may involve familiar objects, so transferring this score into action-risk estimation requires navigation-specific labels and tests.

key_findings.claim: Sections 3–4 adapt Stable Video Diffusion to panoramic exploration. The system first rotates the sphere geometrically, then generates a forward video segment. The spherical-consistency objective (Eq. 2) decodes generated latents, rotates predicted and target panoramas together, re-encodes them and penalizes their latent difference alongside ordinary diffusion loss. An LLM proposes orientation/distance and reasons over generated views. GenEx-DB contains four synthetic visual styles; Street View and Behavior Vision Suite provide held-out domains. Equation 4 describes belief updates using imagined observations, but a calibrated posterior-inference algorithm is not established. Generated views are samples from the model conditioned on available evidence; they are not additional camera measurements.

Table 1, p. 8: FVD is 69.5 for the full method, 81.9 without spherical consistency and 196.7 for six-view generation. IELC measures Inception-feature error after 1,000 closed imagined loops. Table 2, p. 9 gives 0.105 on street scenes and 0.092 indoors, so a blanket claim that both are below 0.1 is inaccurate. GenEx-EQA contains more than 200 synthetic scenarios and uses GPT-4 o as a judge for logic scoring. These are generated-world/QA evaluations, not R2R success or physical navigation deployment.

DEDUCTION: conditional on a fixed real history and model, self-generated samples add computation but no independent observational information about the actual hidden state. Counting them as independent likelihood evidence can create unwarranted certainty. A consistently false generated world can satisfy loop closure. Facts about an occluded physical hazard require a real observation or an explicitly justified prior.

key_findings.claim: Section 3 pp. 3–6: frozen CLIP ViT-B/32 grid features are backprojected with depth/pose into an incremental 3D feature cloud (Eq. 1–3). For a candidate camera ray, k-nearest cloud features plus relative position/orientation/scale feed an MLP predicting feature vector and volume density; volumetric compositing gives region embeddings (Eq. 4–8). Empty neighborhoods skip the MLP. A four-layer view Transformer inpaints contextual information in feature space; region/view cosine losses match CLIP targets, with RGB-D rendering auxiliary loss (Eq. 9–12). HNR pretraining uses 800 HM3D training scenes and random 15-step episodes. Candidate 12-view features and predicted depth generate next-level waypoint/lookahead nodes. A panorama encoder and graph-aware cross-modal Transformer score visited, candidate, lookahead and stop nodes. Branch scores are max (candidate, descendant scores), Eq. 15. Soft-target cross-entropy supervises the branch leading closest to the goal; Dijkstra plus a controller executes the chosen reachable waypoint. This is explicit inference-time feature lookahead, not merely a training loss.

PAPER EXPERIMENT: Table 3 p. 7 holds lookahead policy constant: single-view SR 57.21/SPL 49.15; NeRF RGB56.55/48.61; image generation 58.35/50.96; HNR60.74/51.27; oracle future features 63.13/54.59. This is stronger mechanism evidence than leaderboard comparison. Removing positional embeddings gives 56.17/48.91; removing region loss 60.20/50.74. Fig. 5 p. 7 reports feature similarity decreasing with prediction distance. Table 1 R2R-CE unseen SR 61/SPL 51 versus ETPNav 57/49; Table 2 RxR-CE56.39/46.73 versus 54.79/44.89. Table 5, p. 8 reports rendering at 11.5 ms on one RTX 3090, versus 169.5 ms without sparse sampling and 42.3 ms without KD-tree search. This is component timing. Table 6 gives SR 60.74 for soft supervision versus 56.72 for the hard-target variant; the authors attribute the latter to occlusion and prediction noise.

Blind-region semantic extrapolation deteriorates with distance, and max over noisy descendant scores can favor an overoptimistic branch. No uncertainty penalty or calibration is included in Eq. 15. Large geometric feature memory and 800-scene pretraining are costs. NavMorph and SC²-WM add adaptation; NavQ replaces rollouts with semantic successor features in a different discrete/object-goal protocol. No evidence here that those eliminate HNR's unseen-occlusion error under equal sensing/data.

key_findings.claim: Sections 3.1–3.3, pp. 3–6: visual features first retrieve recent episodic features using attention with relative spatial/time cues and temporal decay; a gate blends current and retrieved representations. An observation-conditioned posterior updates latent s_t. A provisional policy proposes an action, and a Transformer prior predicts its next latent mean. Equation 9 defines Δ_t = predicted s_(t+1) − s_t. A learned residual/gating network ψ(s_t,Δ_t) produces a refined current state, from which the final policy selects the executed action. This Δ is an endogenous predicted state change, not an observed next-state prediction error, and the paper explicitly says it is not a target to minimize. Training combines teacher action cross-entropy on original/refined states (Eq. 11), posterior/prior KL (Eq. 12), and decoded future-feature squared error (Eq. 13). Test-time adaptation compares provisional versus final action distributions by KL, uses a running percentile plus a low-entropy condition, and updates world-model parameters through reconstruction loss (Eq. 14); policy parameters are excluded according to the text. Thus there are separate immediate inference refinement and gradient adaptation mechanisms.

PAPER EXPERIMENT: Table 3 p. 8, monocular R2R-CE val-unseen: reproduced base SR 43.77/SPL 29.39; state correction 48.34/33.02; plus visual calibration 49.86/36.05; full 50.90/37.17; fixed-interval adaptation 50.30/36.58; removing reconstruction 48.89/34.58. Table 1 p. 7 HNR panoramic base 61/51 to 66/54, test 58/50 to 62/53. Training is reported on one RTX3090, under 40 hours (p. 8); no runtime independently measured.

The feedback signal can be large for a correct motion and small for an incorrect but stationary latent prediction; low action entropy does not imply correctness. Algorithm 2 p. 6 uses d (predicted s_(t+1)) versus current calibrated v_t, whereas Eq. 13 and prose use next observation v_(t+1). Timing/target discrepancy requires source-level resolution before implementation. Also distinguish dynamic percentile described in text from fixed τ notation in Algorithm 2. These are methodological/reproducibility uncertainties, not demonstrated benchmark failures.
